CCGL9065 · 26 Fall · Portfolio P01

Who Should Pay for Pollution? Corporate Responsibility and Climate Justice in Hong Kong

When I go shopping for clothes in Causeway Bay, I often come across T-shirts labelled as “sustainable”. At first, I viewed sustainable shopping as a straightforward way to reduce my environmental impact. However, after taking CCGL 9065, I now recognize that consumers cannot make fully informed decisions when companies control how environmental information is presented. This gap between what consumers believe they are buying and the hidden environmental costs of production needs to be addressed. I believe meaningful climate action requires not only individual efforts but also companies taking responsibility for their products' environmental impacts. Although the examples that will be discussed are global, Hong Kong's regulatory framework provides a useful perspective on strengthening corporate responsibility.

Our Week 3 discussion of fashion and product life cycles showed that a product’s environmental impact does not end when consumers discard it. Life Cycle Assessment evaluates impacts across a product’s life, but its results depend on the system boundary defining which processes are included (International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2006). H&M’s sustainability marketing illustrates the risk of greenwashing in the fashion industry. In 2022, Norway's Consumer Authority cautioned H&M that using the Higg Materials Sustainability Index to support environmental claims in garment marketing could be considered misleading, as such claims might not adequately represent a garment's overall environmental impact (Norwegian Consumer Authority, 2022). Recycled materials may reduce some impacts, but they do not themselves account for production, transportation, pollution, or disposal. The case shows how a sustainability label can conceal a wider footprint and prevent consumers from making informed purchasing decisions.

Hong Kong already has a framework that can be expanded. The Product Eco-Responsibility Ordinance (Cap. 603) provides for Producer Responsibility Schemes, based on the “polluter pays” principle. Existing schemes cover plastic shopping bags, waste electrical and electronic equipment, and glass beverage containers. Under the glass-container scheme, suppliers must register, submit returns and audit reports, and pay a recycling levy (Environmental Protection Department [EPD], n.d.). In July 2025, the Legislative Council passed a common framework to facilitate PRSs for additional products (EPD, n.d.). Hong Kong should use this framework to introduce a textile scheme requiring producers to fund collection and recycling, with higher fees for products that are harder to reuse or recycle. Critics may argue that these costs raise product prices or burden small businesses. However, fees should reflect the difficulty of recycling different materials, rather than functioning as a flat tax. The goal is not to punish consumers, but to stop producers shifting disposal costs onto society.

The same transfer of responsibility appears on a much larger scale in the fossil-fuel industry. InfluenceMap (2024) linked 57 corporate and state entities to approximately 80% of global CO₂ emissions from these industries between 2016 and 2022. More concerningly, ExxonMobil's scientists had produced projections that accurately anticipated global warming, while the company’s later public communications were inconsistent with its internal scientific knowledge (Supran et al., 2023). This connects to our Week 7 discussion of truth and manufactured doubt: when companies conceal what they know, the public is left to bear both the environmental consequences and the confusion.

Hong Kong’s climate-disclosure rules are a useful start, but information must lead to accountability. From financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2025, all Main Board issuers must disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions. Broader climate-related disclosures are being phased in, with mandatory reporting for large-cap issuers from 2026 (Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited [SEHK], 2024). Disclosure makes corporate emissions more visible, but it does not itself pay for the damage. Therefore, Hong Kong should build on the polluter-pays principle by requiring major polluters to contribute to an independently monitored environmental remediation fund according to their verified emissions and waste. Such accountability would ensure polluters bear the costs of their actions and help finance environmental restoration and support affected communities.

Ultimately, the problem is not that consumers do too little; it is that those with the greatest power to prevent pollution can shift its costs onto everyone else. Meaningful climate action cannot happen if major corporations continue to use narrow assessment boundaries, conceal their environmental footprint, and contribute to public doubt. From a Hong Kong perspective, extending producer responsibility to textiles and requiring major polluters to help finance environmental recovery are practical ways to address this problem. Climate action should not leave consumers carrying the burden alone. It must reach those with the power to design, produce and profit.
